# Protein function {#sec-protein-function}

::: {.callout-note title="From the exam description"}
Classifications, prediction methods, and definitions.
:::

## Introduction

Predicting what a protein does is the ultimate goal of most sequence
analysis, but "function" is hard to define. It can mean the molecular
activity (e.g. "serine protease"), the biological process the protein
takes part in (e.g. "blood coagulation"), or where in the cell it acts.
The Gene Ontology formalises these three aspects as directed acyclic
graphs of terms. Each annotation carries an *evidence code* that tells
whether it comes from an experiment or was inferred computationally
[@ashburner2000; @go2023]. Enzymes are also classified by EC numbers.
Only a small fraction of all known proteins has experimentally determined
function. Almost everything else is predicted.

The most common approach is **transfer by homology**: if a protein is
similar enough to one of known function, it probably shares that
function [@whisstock2003]. This works well at high sequence identity, but
it becomes unreliable for distant homologs and for paralogs, which often
diverge in function after duplication (@sec-evolution). It also fails for
multidomain proteins, where the matching region may cover only one
domain. Domain- and family-based annotation, for example with Pfam and
InterPro, assigns function at the level of the domain. Structure can show
function even when sequence similarity is lost, for example through
conserved active-site geometry. AlphaFold models have made this possible
for whole proteomes.

Other methods use information beyond the sequence of a single protein.
*Genomic context* methods use comparative genomics. Proteins that are
fused into one chain in another organism (the "Rosetta stone" approach),
that are encoded next to each other across many genomes, or that are
present and absent in the same species (*phylogenetic profiles*) are
likely to be functionally linked
[@marcotte1999science; @marcotte1999nature; @enright2001; @snel2000].
Networks of interactions and co-expression support "guilt by
association" (@sec-protein-interactions). Structure-based interactome
predictions have been used to annotate whole proteomes [@garzon2016].

Some aspects of function can be predicted directly from sequence signals.
*Subcellular localisation* is largely determined by sorting signals.
Secretory signal peptides were first predicted with weight matrices
[@vonheijne1986] and later with neural networks [@nielsen1997]. A key
problem was to separate them from transmembrane helices
[@petersen2011]. Modern predictors such as SignalP 6 and DeepLoc 2 use
protein language models [@teufel2022; @almagro2017; @thumuluri2022]. A
growing application is predicting the effect of *missense variants*.
Unsupervised models of evolutionary sequence variation, and models that
also use structure, can now classify most possible human missense
variants [@frazer2021; @cheng2023].

Evaluating function prediction is difficult. Annotations are incomplete,
biased towards well-studied proteins and change over time. The CAFA
experiments address this by predicting functions for proteins that are
annotated later [@radivojac2013; @zhou2019]. They show steady but modest
progress, and that simple homology-based baselines are hard to beat.

## Key concepts

- Definitions of function; Gene Ontology (MF, BP, CC), evidence codes, EC numbers
- Annotation transfer by homology: identity thresholds, domain architecture, orthologs vs. paralogs, error propagation
- Family/domain-based annotation (Pfam, InterPro)
- Genomic-context methods: gene fusion (Rosetta stone), gene neighbourhood, phylogenetic profiles
- Network-based function prediction (guilt by association; see @sec-protein-interactions)
- Structure-based function prediction
- Sorting signals and subcellular localisation: signal peptides, transmembrane regions, SignalP, DeepLoc
- Variant effect prediction: conservation, unsupervised models (EVE), AlphaMissense
- Critical assessment: CAFA; why function prediction is hard to evaluate

## Key papers

::: {.callout-tip}
★ = mandatory in earlier reading lists.
:::

### Reviews — start here

- @whisstock2003 — prediction of protein function from sequence and structure.
- @radivojac2013 — CAFA: large-scale evaluation of function prediction.
- @zhou2019 — CAFA3.

### Ontologies

- @ashburner2000 — the Gene Ontology.
- @go2023 — the Gene Ontology knowledgebase in 2023.

### Genomic context and non-homology methods

- @marcotte1999science — detecting function and interactions from genome sequences (Rosetta stone).
- @marcotte1999nature — a combined algorithm for genome-wide function prediction.
- @tsoka2000 — metabolic enzymes are frequently involved in gene fusion.
- @enright2001 — functional associations from exhaustive detection of gene fusions.
- @snel2000 — gene fusion versus gene fission.
- @doolittle1999 — "Do you dig my groove?" (commentary on the above).
- ★ @garzon2016 — a computational interactome and functional annotation of the human proteome.

### Sorting signals and localisation

- @vonheijne1986 — a new method for predicting signal-sequence cleavage sites.
- @nielsen1997 — SignalP: neural-network prediction of signal peptides.
- @petersen2011 — SignalP 4.0: discriminating signal peptides from transmembrane regions.
- @teufel2022 — SignalP 6.0: all types of signal peptides with protein language models.
- ★ @almagro2017 — DeepLoc: subcellular localisation with deep learning.
- @thumuluri2022 — DeepLoc 2.0.

### Variant effect prediction

- @frazer2021 — EVE: disease variant prediction from evolutionary data.
- @cheng2023 — AlphaMissense.
